risk_of_bias.note: Well blinded and randomized, but 21% of those enrolled were lost and only completers analysed, the interval between sessions is unreported, drinking after the session was uncontrolled, and analyses beyond the primary outcome are inconsistently described.

indirectness.note: Low doses at one timing during supervised drinking to a fixed target, unlike most real drinking occasions.

imprecision.note: Medians without intervals in 49 people; ranges are wide and a moderate effect cannot be excluded.

rate.reasoning: A randomized, double-blind crossover trial starts high; downgraded for risk of bias, indirectness and twice for imprecision, giving very low. The relation is insufficient evidence because no interval excludes a meaningful effect. The benefit in women is not part of the claim's finding: it is a subgroup difference among several uncorrected tests, with men scoring worse on NAC. The published correction changes only an Introduction passage and does not affect these results. Single study.
rate.population: 49 healthy adults (31 men, 18 women; predominantly white, mostly aged 20 to 30) without alcohol use disorder who completed both sessions, at one US hospital
rate.exposure: N-acetylcysteine capsules at low doses, taken during a supervised session of beer drinking (doses and timing are on the study card)
rate.comparator: Identical lactose placebo capsules taken by the same people during another session with the same drinking target
rate.outcome: Next-morning Hangover Symptoms Scale total score; headache, nausea and weakness; side effects
rate.magnitude: Medians, no intervals: total score 10 against 13 (P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum); headache 1 against 1 (P = 0.93); nausea 0 against 1 (P = 0.11); weakness 1 against 1 (P = 0.72); five-item subset 5 against 5.5 (P = 0.86). Difference scores by sex (NAC minus placebo): women −3.5, men +2 (P = 0.04); nausea P = 0.05, weakness P = 0.03, headache P = 0.32. Side effects after NAC: gastrointestinal 4, headache 2, rash 1, muscle twitches 1, insomnia 1; after placebo: headache 3, gastrointestinal 1.
rate.short: It hasn't been shown. In a trial, 49 young adults drank beer twice, once with NAC and once with dummy pills. Next morning, hangovers weren't clearly different.
rate.rate: One small trial that gave only middle scores, with no margin of error, so a real effect can't be ruled out. It tested low doses at one timing, and drinking after people left wasn't controlled.

risk_of_bias.note: Correlations in which people who felt worse drank more water (confounding by indication), a post hoc re-analysis by the authors of their own data, and remedy ratings without a comparison; source is a narrative review.

indirectness.note: A long walk in the heat, old laboratory studies in a few men, and ratings of perceived efficacy rather than measured effects of water.

imprecision.note: Not applicable: no estimate of the effect of water exists.

rate.reasoning: Observational evidence summarized in a narrative review starts low; downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). It complements the later small trial of water during drinking, which found no detectable effect (Imai et al., 2026, a separate claim). The authors' conclusion that water is not effective is not adopted: no trial existed, so the finding is that the question is untested.
rate.population: Adults with a hangover: 176 walkers in Crete (authors' re-analysis), Dutch students (surveys) and small groups of men in old laboratory studies
rate.exposure: Drinking water during a hangover day (amount self-reported) or as a remedy during or after drinking (survey ratings)
rate.comparator: People who drank less water on the same walk (correlation); no untreated comparison in the surveys
rate.outcome: Hangover severity and thirst ratings and their change during the day; perceived efficacy of water; markers of dehydration
rate.magnitude: Water drunk against hangover severity before, during and after the walk: r = 0.176, 0.243 and 0.229 (p from 0.019 to below 0.001); against change in hangover severity r = 0.103 (p = 0.174), 0.017 (p = 0.828) and 0.066 (p = 0.388); against thirst and change in thirst |r| no more than 0.061, none significant. Survey efficacy ratings for water 5.2 to 5.8 out of 10. Thirst above an alcohol-free day only at the 09:30 and 10:30 ratings; hangover above it at every rating to 15:30.
rate.short: It seems not. Thirst was clearly up only in the morning, but the hangover lasted all day. Up to mid-2024, no experiment had tested water as a fix.
rate.rate: It's all from one review: a walk in the heat where people who felt worse drank more water, students' own ratings, and small, old lab studies of men. No experiment tested water itself.

risk_of_bias.note: Trials (card sc_van_nhat_2026): 14 of 15 at some concerns or high risk of bias by the review's RoB 2 figure, mainly from deviations from the intended interventions and missing outcome data; every outcome self-reported; attrition up to 95%; no sensitivity analysis by risk of bias. Observational studies (card sc_pearson_2013): strategies and outcomes self-reported, nearly always at the same sitting, mostly cross-sectional, unappraised, the review's author a co-author of 7 of the 62 studies.

inconsistency.note: The trial estimates for drinking and problems agree (I² 0% to 22%). The observational findings point different ways by strategy and design (less drinking between people, more on days with some strategies), which the status 'mixed' records; the very heterogeneous effect on reported strategy use (I² 98%) is not a drinking outcome. Not rated down, because the graded finding rests on the trials.

indirectness.note: No trial isolated a single strategy: strategies were taught in bundles, often with personalized normative feedback, against a mix of controls, so the effect of the strategies themselves, or of strategies people choose on their own, is not measured; almost all participants were young US university students.

imprecision.note: The intervals for quantity, frequency and problems are narrow and exclude more than a small effect (none goes beyond −0.19); the problems estimate reaches no difference.

publication_bias.note: No funnel asymmetry in any pool, though with 6 to 9 trials the tests have little power; English-language peer-reviewed reports only, without trial registries or grey literature. Not rated down.

rate.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down for risk of bias (14 of 15 trials at some concerns or high risk, self-reported outcomes) and indirectness (bundles taught with other components, not single strategies; US students), giving low for what the trials show: teaching bundles of strategies changed reported drinking very little. The relation stays insufficient evidence for the claim's question, whether the strategies themselves lower drinking or harms: no trial tested any single strategy, the bundles' effects are very small and partly attributable to other components, and the observational associations, which by themselves would be very low (narrative review only), point different ways by design. The meta-analysis is AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional: its list of excluded studies is in an appendix not read), searched English-language peer-reviewed reports only, and its abstract leads with estimates made after dropping a trial; its PRISMA counts do not add up (564 records by database against 514 printed). Counted once: Larimer et al. (2007) and Sugarman and Carey (2009), described in the 2013 review, are among the meta-analysis's trials. Status mixed: the observational findings differ in direction by strategy and design, with only the review author's untested explanation, while the trials show very small or no effects. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review.
rate.population: College students and young adults: 15 randomized trials (2007 to 2023), 13 at US universities, one at a Swedish university and one Australian pilot, mostly undergraduates aged 18 to 24 (15,714 randomized and 6,587 analysed, editors' calculation); and college students in 62 published quantitative studies found up to February 2013 (some samples appear in more than one study; countries not reported in the review), including incoming students, athletes, women and students sent to alcohol programmes, as summarized by one narrative review
rate.exposure: Protective behavioural strategies taught or prompted in randomized trials, as bundles (limiting or stopping drinking, manner of drinking such as pacing, harm reduction such as a designated driver), alone or within multi-component interventions, mostly brief and digital; and self-reported use of strategies in observational studies, measured with at least 11 questionnaires in many versions (most often the Protective Behavioral Strategies Survey): strategies used just before, during or after drinking, such as setting a limit or leaving at a set time, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, drinking water, eating, avoiding drinking games or mixing types of alcohol, keeping track of drinks, using a designated driver or going home with a friend; 13 of the 62 studies also counted avoiding drinking altogether
rate.comparator: In trials: assessment only, no intervention, education or other active or attention controls, or the same intervention without a strategies booster; in observational studies: students reporting fewer strategies (between people, mostly cross-sectional), days without a given strategy (within people, two studies), control groups in trials of brief interventions, where strategy use was a measured mediator, not what was randomized, and no instruction to use strategies (one experiment)
rate.outcome: Self-reported alcohol use (quantity, frequency, heavy drinking, estimated blood alcohol), alcohol-related problems and reported strategy use
rate.magnitude: Van Nhat et al. (2026), random effects, Hedges' g at the longest follow-up (3 days to 12 months): quantity −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), 9 trials, I² 22.0%, prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07; frequency −0.09 (−0.17 to −0.02), 6 trials, I² 11.85%, prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001; problems −0.07 (−0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%, and −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01) without Larimer et al. (2007); reported strategy use 0.58 (−0.21 to 1.37), 6 trials, I² 97.8%, prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63, and 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), I² 49.9%, without O'Donnell et al. (2019). Subgroups, without between-subgroup tests (intervals only in supplements): follow-up over 3 months, quantity −0.12 and frequency −0.13; strategies as an adjunct, quantity −0.10 and frequency −0.13; as a core or primary component, no significant effect on quantity. Risk of bias: 1 trial low, 10 some concerns, 4 high (Fig. 2). Mediation through strategy use in 3 or 4 of 6 trials. Pearson (2013): no pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: nearly every study found that students reporting more strategies reported drinking less and/or fewer problems; with one questionnaire, correlations with drinking were negative on a how-often-when-drinking scale and positive on a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions (3 studies); a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; in one sample followed for 12 months, prospective correlations with drinking similar to same-time ones, change in some kinds of strategy use predicting less drinking or fewer problems, and 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant; day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).
rate.short: Nobody knows yet. No trial tested one habit alone. And teaching students a bundle of them barely changed how they said they drank.
rate.rate: The trials agree, but 14 of 15 had weaknesses, every result was self-reported, and nearly all were US students. Habits were taught in bundles, often with other parts, so no single habit was tested.

risk_of_bias.note: Not rated: the study has no data on the outcome.

indirectness.note: A registry of harms in people who reached care, not a study of withdrawal relief.

rate.reasoning: No study read measured whether loperamide relieves opioid withdrawal; the only source records why 6 people took it and the harms seen in those who reached a toxicologist. Observational, so it starts low; indirectness -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. The claim states that the question is untested in what was read, not that loperamide does not work.
rate.population: People who take loperamide to avoid or relieve opioid withdrawal (6 of 26 registry cases seen by US medical toxicologists)
rate.comparator: No loperamide, or withdrawal medicines (no data)
rate.magnitude: No data: relief of withdrawal was not recorded. 6 of the 12 misuse cases (26 in all) had taken loperamide to avoid withdrawal; their outcomes are not reported separately.
rate.short: We can't say yet. The one study we read counted 26 people seen by poisons doctors after taking it. Six took it to avoid withdrawal; nobody recorded if it helped.
rate.rate: One small registry of people who needed a poisons doctor. It never measured whether withdrawal eased, and it had no one to compare with.

risk_of_bias.note: Forum content, qualitative accounts, one ethnographic account, a survey's recommendation and two test-strip studies of reported behaviour (a before-and-after pilot without controls and an observational study); no comparison of people using a practice with people not using it; none appraised by the review (card sc_morrison_2025).

indirectness.note: Second-hand through a scoping review; practices described, not measured as exposures with harm as an outcome.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed; peer-led and grey literature were not searched, which the claim states.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive and qualitative sources start low; rated down for risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low. The claim rests only on a scoping review, a narrative synthesis without appraisal, so it stays at draft and its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3). That no practice has been tested is itself the finding (decision p-before-during-after); section 7, findings only, held for the senior author. Status single study: one review.
rate.population: People who use benzodiazepines, including novel ones, in forum, qualitative, ethnographic, survey, pilot and observational sources gathered by one scoping review: posters on a Swedish drug forum; 45 women and gender-diverse people who use drugs in British Columbia; one participant in Melbourne; 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok; 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore; 541 adults who use drugs in several US states
rate.exposure: Practices people use themselves before or during use, as described: limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they use, avoiding alcohol at the same time, comparing vendors and batches, peer check-ins, not using or injecting alone; and reported behaviour after a test-strip result (asking someone to check on them, using smaller amounts, taking turns, keeping naloxone nearby)
rate.comparator: None: no source compared people using a practice with people not using it; the two test-strip studies compared reports before and after receiving strips, or related behaviour to the strip result
rate.outcome: Any harm, such as overdose, assault, injury or arrest (not measured against a comparison in any source); reported behaviour after a test-strip result
rate.magnitude: No source compared people who used a practice with people who did not, and none measured harm. Behaviour after test strips: in a before-and-after pilot (68 of 103 followed up at one month, no control group), reported using alone was 96% before and 68% after, and 69% reported a harm reduction behaviour after a result; in an observational study of 541 adults over 28 days, a positive result went with using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (sizes given only in the review's table, second-hand).
rate.short: Nobody knows yet. People describe habits like staying home or not drinking with benzos. But a 2025 review found no study of whether any lowers harm.
rate.rate: It's second-hand, from one review that didn't judge its sources: forum posts, people's accounts, a survey and two test-strip studies. None tested whether a habit lowers harm.

risk_of_bias.note: Helpfulness is the respondent's own retrospective judgment, recorded at the same sitting as the outcome, sometimes years later, in self-selected samples, with no adjustment (cards sc_wood_2024 and sc_simonsson_2023, overall very high); the review's figures are second-hand (sc_piercey_2024).

inconsistency.note: The two surveys, with different lists and questions, agree that a calming or accepting response was the one most often named as helpful.

indirectness.note: Worded as what people say helped, not as what works.

rate.reasoning: Cross-sectional self-report starts low; down two for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated refers to the reports only: two independent surveys (University College London; a Karolinska, Oxford and Wisconsin team), with different lists and questions, agree that a calming or accepting response was the one most often named as helpful; no study tested whether any response works. Section 7 (decision p-before-during-after): findings only, for the senior author's approval.
rate.population: Adults who have used classic psychedelics and recalled a challenging experience: a self-selected online sample (529), retreat attendees chosen for personal change after difficult ceremonies (16) and a US online panel (613, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience)
rate.exposure: Responses during a challenging experience (accepting, observing, lying down, calming the mind, changing place, people or music, asking for help, taking another drug), as respondents recalled them and judged their helpfulness
rate.comparator: None: no comparison of people who used a response with people who did not
rate.outcome: Self-judged helpfulness during the experience; emotional breakthrough rated afterwards (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory)
rate.magnitude: No effect estimates. Tried and judged helpful (Wood et al., 2024; n = 529): letting go 84.5%, observing the mind 77.3%, closing the eyes or lying down 73.9%; least often anger 9.4%, trying to sleep 9.7%, telling it to stop 10.6%, another drug or alcohol 12.1%. Count of the 11 responses grouped as acceptance and reappraisal judged helpful, against emotional breakthrough rated at the same sitting: r = 0.50. Ticked as helpful (Simonsson et al., 2023; n = 613, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience): calming the mind 41.9%, changing location 27.4%, asking a friend 20.2%, changing the people around 20.2%, cannabis 18.4%, changing the music 16.2%, alcohol 8.8%, another drug 3.6%. The two surveys' percentages are not comparable (different lists, questions and denominators). Second-hand (Piercey et al., 2024): 91% used strategies, rated modestly effective; 65.9% of helpline callers found it helpful.
rate.short: Looking back, people most often say accepting it or calming the mind helped; 85 in 100 found letting go helpful in one survey. None of it was tested.
rate.rate: Only what people remembered, sometimes years later, in people who chose to answer, with nothing tested. Two separate surveys agree on what's named most, but they asked different questions.

risk_of_bias.note: Recalled practices (first experiences a median of three and a half years earlier) weighted by the respondents' own importance ratings and including practices after the experience, outcomes rated at the same sitting, no adjustment, survivor bias (card sc_palmer_2022, overall very high); the panel survey's item is a retrospective attribution, ticked at the same sitting as the challenge rating (sc_simonsson_2023).

inconsistency.note: The first-experience correlation and the attribution point the same way; the non-significant most-recent correlation is stated.

imprecision.note: Intervals given; the claim is worded as insufficient evidence.

rate.reasoning: Cross-sectional self-report starts low; down two for risk of bias, giving very low. Status single study: the habits-experience association rests on one survey; the panel survey's item is a different measure (an attribution of the worst experience), and the review adds no primary data and misreports the survey, so it is cited only for what it adds. Section 7 (decision p-before-during-after): findings only, for the senior author's approval.
rate.population: People who use classic psychedelics outside research or therapy: a self-selected survey of experienced people (163) and a US online panel (613); a mini review of the literature
rate.exposure: Harm reduction practices before, during and after use, recalled and weighted by importance; having had no preparation, as a respondent's own explanation of their most challenging experience
rate.comparator: People who recalled fewer or less highly rated practices; respondents who did not link their most challenging experience to having had no preparation
rate.outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), emotional breakthrough (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory), thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others
rate.magnitude: Palmer and Maynard (2022), n = 163: importance-weighted practice score and challenge r = −0.21 (95% CI −0.35 to −0.06) for the first experience, −0.15 (−0.30 to 0.00) for the most recent; with breakthrough r = 0.24 (0.09 to 0.38) on both (editors' intervals; 2% to 6% of the variation). Score 40.06 first against 48.68 most recent; challenge 17.14 against 17.29 per cent of the maximum. Simonsson et al. (2023): no preparation linked to the most challenging experience by 182 of 613; challenge standardized beta 0.09; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others adjusted OR 1.17 (0.56 to 2.45).
rate.short: Nobody can say yet. In one survey of 163 people, a higher safety-habit score went with a slightly easier first trip. Not clearly with the latest one, though.
rate.rate: One survey of memories, with habits after the trip counted and nothing else taken into account. People who quit after a hard first trip couldn't take part, and a review found little other research.

risk_of_bias.note: No comparison group; whether people stopped was recorded for 27 of 113; the authors infer stopping from improvement in one case.

inconsistency.note: The two longest follow-ups and earlier series point in different directions, but there is no comparative estimate to be inconsistent.

imprecision.note: No comparative data; lutein given to 5 people.

rate.reasoning: Observational case data start low; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Stopping poppers and lutein are what people with this diagnosis were told to do, but no report compared them with not doing so; the improvement seen in many followed-up cases may be the natural course. The claim states findings only (section 7).
rate.population: People diagnosed with eye damage after poppers use (113 published cases, 2004 to 2021)
rate.exposure: Stopping poppers use, or oral lutein
rate.comparator: Continuing use, or no lutein (no comparison group in the reports)
rate.outcome: Recovery of vision and of retinal findings
rate.magnitude: No comparative data. Stopping advised for 42 of the 45 with treatment documented; lutein for 5 (3 with stopping, 2 alone); compliance recorded for 27 (19 compliant); OCT improved or resolved in 46 of 75 followed up, without data by stopping.
rate.short: Nobody knows yet. Eye scans improved in 46 of 75 people checked again, but no report compared stopping with carrying on, and only 5 got lutein.
rate.rate: Case reports pooled by one review, with no comparison group. Whether people stopped was recorded for 27 of 113, lutein went to 5, and the improvement may have come anyway.

risk_of_bias.note: Not rated: there are no outcome data on the question.

indirectness.note: The only statement on the question is the review authors' second-hand remark about reviews in palliative care.

rate.reasoning: The question matters in real life (ordinary laxatives are what most people try first), but the sources read hold no data on it: the meta-analysis did not include such laxatives, and its authors' remark is second-hand. Starting low because no randomized evidence on the question was read; indirectness -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. The Cochrane review the authors cite (Candy et al. 2015, doi:10.1002/14651858.CD003448.pub4) is the source to read next.
rate.population: People with opioid-induced constipation (the review's trials were mostly in people taking opioids for chronic pain)
rate.comparator: Placebo, or prescription medicines for opioid-induced constipation
rate.magnitude: No data in the review read: no over-the-counter laxative trial was included. The authors' remark that their effect is hard to assess cites two Cochrane reviews in palliative care (Candy et al. 2011 and 2015), not read.
rate.short: We can't say yet. The one review we read covered only prescription medicines. Its authors say studies of laxatives from the shop are hard to judge.
rate.rate: There's no data on this in what we read: the review didn't include shop laxatives, and its authors' remark is second-hand, from two reviews of laxatives in palliative care.

risk_of_bias.note: No control group; children selected for long sleep onset invite regression to the mean; parents knew the programme had begun.

inconsistency.note: Single study; diary and actigraph agree.

indirectness.note: Worded for the children and setting studied.

imprecision.note: About 28 children; the before-after change is precise but its cause is not.

rate.reasoning: An uncontrolled before-after comparison starts low; risk of bias −1 gives very low. Status single study.
rate.population: Children aged 6 to 14 with ADHD on stable stimulant medicine taking more than 60 minutes to fall asleep, in a hospital ADHD programme
rate.exposure: A sleep-hygiene programme: a consistent bedtime and waking time, no caffeine and no naps, reviewed with parents from sleep diaries (study conditions in the study card)
rate.comparator: The same children's sleep in the nights before the programme (no control group)
rate.outcome: Time to fall asleep (parent diaries and actigraphy), night-to-night variability, clinician-rated improvement, ADHD symptoms
rate.magnitude: Sleep-onset latency 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on diaries (t(28) = 2.77, p = .01) and 98.1 to 73.0 on actigraphy (t(21) = 2.92, p < .01); effect size 0.67; diary variability 47.7 to 29.1 minutes; 5 children below 60 minutes; clinicians: 21% much or very much improved, 54% unchanged.
rate.short: Maybe a little. In one study, children fell asleep in 69 minutes on average with a set routine, down from 92. Only 5 of about 28 got under an hour.
rate.rate: One small study, comparing children only with their own sleep before. Children were picked when sleep was at its worst, and there was no comparison group, so some of the gain may have come anyway.

item.statement: NAC pills have been shown to stop hangovers.
item.why: In the one trial, 49 young adults' next-morning hangovers weren't clearly different on NAC than on dummy pills. One small trial can't rule out an effect, either.

lines.short: It hasn't been shown. In a trial, 49 young adults drank beer twice, once with NAC and once with dummy pills. Next morning, hangovers weren't clearly different.
lines.but: It's one small trial, and it couldn't rule out a real effect. Drinking after people went home wasn't checked.
how: 49 healthy adults, mostly white and in their twenties, drank beer twice under watch at a US hospital. In random order, they took NAC once and look-alike dummy pills once. Neither they nor the staff knew which was which.

Next morning, the middle hangover score was 10 with NAC and 13 with dummy pills, on a scale from 0 to 52. A gap that size could easily be chance. Headache, nausea and weakness didn't clearly differ either.
Women's scores were 3.5 points lower on NAC than on dummy pills, and men's 2 points higher. That was one of several comparisons not corrected for chance, so it needs a trial designed to test it.

Side effects were few and mild with both. After NAC there were 4 cases of gut trouble, 2 of headache, and one each of rash, muscle twitches and poor sleep; after dummy pills, 3 of headache and 1 of gut trouble.

item.statement: A hangover is just being dried out, so drinking water fixes it.
item.why: Thirst was clearly up only in the morning, while the hangover lasted all day. And up to mid-2024, no experiment had tested water as a fix.

lines.short: It seems not. Thirst was clearly up only in the morning, but the hangover lasted all day. Up to mid-2024, no experiment had tested water as a fix.
lines.but: It all comes through one review, partly its authors' second look at their own data. None of it tested what water does.
how: A 2024 review found no experiment, up to July 2024, that tested if water stops or eases a hangover.

On a long walk in Crete, 176 people with a hangover said how much water they drank. Those who drank more had worse hangovers, but the amount wasn't linked to how much their hangover or thirst changed over the day. The review's authors re-analysed this from their own data.
In surveys of Dutch students, water was the most used hangover remedy. They rated how well it worked at about 5 to 6 out of 10, with nothing to compare it against.

After a night of heavy drinking, people were clearly thirstier than on a day without alcohol only in the morning, but the hangover lasted all day. Small old studies found mild, brief changes in body fluids. So the authors see being dried out and a hangover as two separate effects of drinking.

item.statement: Trials show that teaching students safer drinking habits cuts how much they drink.
item.why: In 15 trials, mostly with US students, how much they said they drank didn't clearly change. No trial tested one habit alone.

lines.short: Nobody knows yet. No trial tested one habit alone. And teaching students a bundle of them barely changed how they said they drank.
lines.but: Nearly all were US college students. And every result is what they said about themselves.
how: A 2026 review pooled 15 trials, published 2007 to 2023, that taught or prompted bundles of habits like keeping track of drinks, pacing or eating. 13 were at US universities, nearly all with students aged 18 to 24. Most programs were short and digital, often mixed with other parts.

Compared with surveys alone, education or other programs, how much students said they drank didn't clearly change. They drank a tiny bit less often. They may have had a tiny bit fewer alcohol problems, but that could be chance.

A 2013 review of 62 studies says that students who reported more habits nearly always also reported drinking less or fewer problems. But most asked about both at one sitting. In one experiment, students told to use more habits said they did, yet didn't drink less.

In two day-by-day studies, students drank less on days they used habits about how they drank, like pacing, but more on days they used habits for limiting or stopping. On days with a designated driver or a friend to go home with, they drank more and had more problems. The author thinks people plan those for heavy nights.

item.statement: Students drank more on days they had a designated driver.
item.why: In two day-by-day studies, they drank more and had more problems on those days. The author thinks people plan a ride home for heavy nights.

lines.short: Nobody knows yet. No trial tested one habit alone. And teaching students a bundle of them barely changed how they said they drank.
lines.but: Nearly all were US college students. And every result is what they said about themselves.

Compared with surveys alone, education or other programs, how much students said they drank didn't clearly change. They drank a tiny bit less often. They may have had a tiny bit fewer alcohol problems, but that could be chance.
